query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled amount of molybdenum into the high-entropy alloy coating will induce the in situ formation of a lubricious Mo oxide (e.g., MoO2) during friction, thereby reducing both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., based on AlCrTiZr) without molybdenum addition that exhibits a typical friction coefficient near 0.72 and a relatively high wear rate.
generation.intervention: Introduce a precise, optimized fraction of molybdenum into the alloy composition during magnetron sputtering to form a Mo-incorporated high-entropy alloy coating.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to be effective over a wide service temperature range (from room temperature up to high temperatures around or above 600°C) under sliding contact and moderate to high normal loads.
generation.structural_mediator: The addition of Mo leads to a modified columnar microstructure where frictional heating promotes the oxidation of Mo at the worn interface, resulting in a thin, in situ lubricious MoO2 layer that facilitates shear.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, localized frictional heating oxidizes the Mo enriched regions to form a MoO2 layer that has a layered, low-shear-strength structure. This layer acts as a solid lubricant, reducing adhesive interactions and mitigating abrasive wear. At the same time, the balance between hardness and toughness in the modified microstructure further contributes to reduced wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the Mo-incorporated coating should exhibit approximately a 50–70% reduction in the friction coefficient and up to an order of magnitude (10×) lower wear rate.
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy coatings without Mo, which typically have a friction coefficient around 0.72 and higher wear rates.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated to hold when the Mo content is optimized to sustain controlled oxide layer formation without adversely affecting the alloy’s overall microstructure; it assumes that operating temperatures are sufficient for Mo oxidation without causing other deleterious phase changes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements and long-term durability of the lubricating oxide layer under prolonged service and variable environmental conditions remain uncertain and may depend on the exact Mo concentration and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy coatings: one set with the optimized Mo addition and a control set without Mo. Subject both sets to identical ball-on-disk sliding tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 600°C under the same normal load conditions.
measurements: Wear rate (e.g., measured via wear volume loss)
Microstructural and chemical analysis of the worn surfaces to detect the presence and continuity of a MoO2-rich layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-incorporated coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the control, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the formation of a lubricious Mo oxide layer at the interface, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The results reveal that the Mo content significantly affects the microstructure, hardness, fracture toughness, and tribological behavior of the coatings. As the Mo content in the coatings increases gradually, the preferred orientation changes from (200) to (111). The coatings consistently exhibit a distinct columnar structure. Additionally, the hardness of the coatings increases from 24.39 to 30.24 GPa, along with an increase in fracture toughness. The friction coefficient is reduced from 0.72 to 0.26, and the wear rate is reduced by 10 times. During the friction process, the inter-column regions of the coatings are initially damaged, causing the wear track to exhibit a wavy pattern. Greater frictional heat is generated at the crest of the wave, resulting in the formation of a MoO2 lubricating layer. The friction reaction helps to reduce the shear force during friction, demonstrating the lower friction coefficient of the (AlCrTiZrMox)N coatings. As is well known, friction between components is the main cause of the failure of mechanical equipment under extreme conditions, such as high speed and high temperature [,]. Based on the data on global energy consumption and economic expenditure, energy losses related to friction-and-wear account for one-third of global energy consumption [,]. Traditionally, the way to reduce friction is usually to use oil or grease lubrication systems []. However, some devices with high cleanliness requirements do not allow the presence of foreign additives such as lubricating oil. Therefore, it is necessary to investigate new materials and lubricating media to reduce friction and wear.
